Step 4 correctly restates the book's actual next step (solve M = ((x_F+x)/2,(y_F+y)/2) using the other known point on the diagonal), which is exactly we13's method. Nothing taught beyond the book; the signal (submitted point equals the known diagonal's midpoint) is precise and would not misdiagnose another error.

misconceptions.label: Rounds n to the nearest year instead of up
misconceptions.description: The student finds n correctly but then rounds it to the nearest whole year in the usual way, so a value such as 19.3 becomes 19 instead of being rounded up to 20.

refutation.text_md: You found $n$ correctly and then rounded it the way you would round any number, to the nearest whole year, so $19.3$ became $19$. Finding $n$ was the hard part and you did it. The last step is the one that is different here: the question says to round up.

Remember what $n$ is. Solving $A=P(1+in)$ for $n$ gives the time at which the money has grown to exactly the goal amount. Investing $\text{R1080}$ at $10.9$ % p.a. to reach $\text{R3348}$ gives $n=19.3$ years.

The money keeps growing the longer it stays invested, so after $19$ years it has not yet reached $\text{R3348}$. The goal is only reached part of the way into the 20th year. The answer has to be a whole number of years, so the first whole number of years that is enough is $20$.
Rounding up means going to the next whole number above whenever $n$ is not already a whole number. So $19.3$ becomes $20$, and $24.9987...$ becomes $25$.
When a question asks you to round up, finish by writing the next whole year above $n$: $19.3$ years means $20$ years.

provenance.verifier_reason: I worked the example through. 3348/1080 = 3.1, then (3.1 - 1)/0.109 = 19.27, which the book writes as 19.3. After 19 years the amount is 1080(1 + 0.109 x 19) = R3316.68, below R3348. After 20 years it is R3434.40, above R3348. So 20 is the first whole year that is enough, and the refutation's claims about 19 and 20 are true. It matches the canonical answer of 20 for this exercise. It also matches the book's treatment of 24.9987... becoming 25, in the same family of exercises. The error is real. The book stresses 'round UP' at the last step, and nearest rounding of 19.3 gives the one-short answer 19. The refutation argues against that specific slip rather than restating the method. It teaches nothing new: the 'money keeps growing' reasoning follows directly from the formula. It names no question id, page or review history. The only q: id sits in the evidence field, not in the student-facing text. The signal is too broad (see signal_ok).

misconceptions.label: Divides $\frac{A}{P}$ by $n$ without taking the 1 away
misconceptions.description: After reaching $\frac{A}{P} = 1 + in$, the student divides by $n$ straight away and never subtracts the 1, so the principal gets counted as interest.
misconceptions.signal: The rate comes out far too large: it equals $\frac{A}{P} \div n$ written as a percentage, for example 32 where the correct rate is 12 for growing R2500 to R4000 in 5 years.

refutation.text_md: You made the right first move: dividing both sides by $P$ gives $\frac{A}{P} = 1 + in$. Then you divided by $n$ straight away, as if all of $\frac{A}{P}$ were interest, and the $1$ was left behind.

In $\frac{A}{P} = 1 + in$, the $1$ is the principal itself coming back, and only $in$ is the interest. For Fritha, $\frac{4000}{2500} = 1.6$ means her money ends up 1.6 times what she put in, so only the extra $0.6$ is interest.

Test what dividing by 5 gives: $\frac{1.6}{5} = 0.32$, a rate of 32 %. Put it back into the formula: $2500(1 + 0.32 \times 5) = 2500 \times 2.6 = 6500$, not R4000. So that rate does not grow R2500 to R4000.

The move that works: from $\frac{A}{P} = 1 + in$, subtract $1$ from both sides to get $\frac{A}{P} - 1 = in$, and only then divide by $n$. For Fritha, $1.6 - 1 = 0.6$ and $0.6 \div 5 = 0.12$, so the rate is 12 % p.a.

provenance.verifier_reason: I worked it through myself. From A/P = 1.6, dividing by 5 gives 0.32, which is 32%. Substituting back gives 2500(1 + 0.32 x 5) = 2500 x 2.6 = 6500, not 4000, so the check is right. The corrected route (1.6 - 1 = 0.6, then 0.6 / 5 = 0.12, so 12% p.a.) matches the worked example and its final answer. The refutation argues against the specific slip: the 1 is the principal, so only the 0.6 is interest. It names no question id, page or review history. The signal (A/P divided by n as a percentage, e.g. 32 for a correct 12) is accurate and would not misdiagnose a student.

misconceptions.label: Uses the interest charged as $A$
misconceptions.description: When the question gives the interest on its own, the student puts that interest in for $A$ instead of adding it to the principal first.
misconceptions.signal: A negative rate, for example about -24.8 for the stove that cost R3750 and was paid off over 3 years with R956.25 interest.

refutation.text_md: You spotted the right formula, $A = P(1 + in)$, and that $n = 3$. The slip is in which amount is $A$: you used the R956.25 of interest, which is only the extra part.
In $A = P(1 + in)$, $A$ is the whole accumulated amount: the starting amount $P$ plus the interest on it. For Bonnie, $A$ is everything she paid in total, not just the interest.

See what the mistake does: $\frac{956.25}{3750} = 0.255$, which is less than $1$. For $1 + in$ to be less than $1$, $i$ would have to be negative, and a negative rate cannot be interest being charged. A negative answer is the sign that $A$ is wrong.

The move that works: when you are given the interest, add it to the principal first. Total paid $= 3750 + 956.25 = 4706.25$, so $A = 4706.25$ and $P = 3750$. Then $1.255 - 1 = 0.255$ and $0.255 \div 3 = 0.085$, which is 8.5 %.

provenance.verifier_reason: I checked the numbers. Using A = 956.25 gives 956.25/3750 = 0.255, then (0.255 - 1)/3 = -0.2483, about -24.8%, so the signal is right. The corrected route (A = 3750 + 956.25 = 4706.25, A/P = 1.255, 0.255/3 = 0.085, so 8.5%) matches the canonical solution step for step. The point that A/P < 1 forces a negative i, which cannot be interest charged, is mathematically sound and argues against this specific slip. The refutation names no question id, page or review history. The line 'a negative answer is the sign that A is wrong' is slightly loose as a general rule, but it is correct in this context and does not teach an error.

misconceptions.label: Uses the later age as the number of years
misconceptions.description: When the question gives the child's age at the deposit and at the end, the student puts the later age in for $n$ instead of the difference between the two ages.
misconceptions.signal: The rate comes out too small, because $n$ was too big: for the deposit made on the son's fifth birthday and checked on his 21st birthday the answer is about 12.4 where the correct rate is 16.25.

refutation.text_md: You rearranged correctly, with $\frac{A}{P} - 1$ divided by $n$. The slip is in what you put in for $n$: you used the child's age at the end, but $n$ is the number of years the money was invested.

The money only started earning interest on the day of the deposit. If it went in on the son's fifth birthday and was counted on his 21st, it was invested for $21 - 5 = 16$ years, which is how the book sets out $n$. The first 5 years of the son's life never earned anything.

Using 21 makes the time too long, so the same growth gets spread over too many years: $\frac{\frac{18000}{5000} - 1}{21} = \frac{2.6}{21} \approx 0.124$, about 12.4 %. The correct rate over 16 years is $\frac{2.6}{16} = 0.1625$, which is 16.25 %.

The move that works: when the question gives two ages, subtract the earlier from the later to get $n$, and write $n = \text{later age} - \text{earlier age}$ in your list of known values before you substitute.

provenance.verifier_reason: I checked the numbers. Using n = 21 gives 2.6/21 = 0.1238, about 12.4%. The correct n = 21 - 5 = 16 gives 2.6/16 = 0.1625, which is 16.25% and matches the canonical answer. The advice to set n = later age - earlier age among the known values is exactly how the book writes it in all six cited solutions. The statement about how the book sets out n is true, because those solutions are book-worked. There is no question id, page number or review history. The signal (rate too small because n is too big, about 12.4 against 16.25) is correct and specific.

misconceptions.label: Rounding part-way through the calculation
misconceptions.description: The student works out $(1+i)^n$ (or another middle value), cuts it to a few decimal places to keep the numbers tidy, and only then multiplies by $P$, so the final amount is slightly off.
misconceptions.signal: The amount is close to the correct accumulated amount but does not match it to the cent.

refutation.text_md: You shortened a long decimal part-way through, probably to keep the working neat. That is a natural thing to do, and writing $A=P(1+i)^n$ with the right $P$, $i$ and $n$ is exactly the right start. The slip comes after that, at the rounding.

The book asks you not to round off until you have reached the solution. The reason is that $(1+i)^n$ is not the answer yet: it still gets multiplied by $P$, and $P$ is a large number. Whatever you cut off from $(1+i)^n$ is multiplied by $P$ too, so a tiny cut turns into a visible difference in rand.

Take the investment of R30 000 at $6\%$ for $4$ years. Here $(1+0.06)^4=1.26247696$. If you shorten that to $1.26$ first, then $30\,000\times 1.26=37\,800$. The book's amount is R37 874.31, which comes from going straight from $30\,000(1+0.06)^4$ to the answer without cutting anything off on the way.
Write $A=P(1+i)^n$, substitute your values, and let the calculator work out the whole line at full length. Round off once, at the very end, to two decimal places.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real for this objective. Four canonical questions in this set (ex9-2-2, ex9-2-3, ex9-7-9, ex9-7-10) carry the instruction 'round your answer to two decimal places, but do not round off until you have reached the solution'. The canonical method is a single-line A=P(1+i)^n evaluated in full, rounded once at the end, and the refutation matches it. I checked the numbers myself: 1.06^2=1.1236 and 1.1236^2=1.26247696. Cutting that to 1.26 gives 30 000x1.26=37 800. The full calculation gives 30 000x1.26247696=37 874.3088, which rounds to 37 874.31, matching the canonical answer of the worked example. The argument targets this specific slip. It explains that a cut in (1+i)^n is multiplied by P, and it does not just restate the method. The worked example it uses states all of its givens, so the student does not need to see another question. The text names no question id, page, figure or review history. It says only 'the book', which is generic and has no id or page. The 'why' (the cut is multiplied by P) is plain arithmetic, not new curriculum. Minor wording points that do not change the verdict: 'a tiny cut' is loose, since 1.26 changes the answer by about R74, and 'P is a large number' holds for every exercise in this set (R800 to R6970). One residual risk: if the tutor ever asks the R30 000 / 6% / 4-year question itself, the refutation reveals its answer. The question set marks that item as a worked example, not an exercise.

misconceptions.label: Picks the account with the bigger rate
misconceptions.description: The student compares the two stated percentage rates and chooses the account with the larger one, without working out the accumulated amounts, so a simple-interest account with a slightly higher rate beats a compound-interest account that actually grows more.
misconceptions.signal: Chooses the account with the larger stated rate (here Bank A at 11%) and gives no accumulated amounts for the two accounts.

refutation.text_md: You compared the two rates, saw that $11\%$ is bigger than $10.5\%$, and picked that account. That is a natural first check, and it works when both accounts earn interest the same way. Here they do not: one pays simple interest and the other pays compound interest.

Simple interest is calculated on the original R1450 only. Compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus the interest already earned, so each year's interest is a little bigger than the year before. That is how a lower rate can still end up ahead.
Bank B, compound interest at $10.5\%$ for $3$ years: $A=P(1+i)^{n}=1450(1+0.105)^{3}=\text{R1956.39}$.
R1956.39 is more than R1928.50, so Bank B leaves Bianca with the highest accumulated balance even though its rate is lower. The two rates alone could not tell you that.

Next time, do not choose on the rate. Work out the accumulated amount for each account with its own formula, $A=P(1+in)$ for simple interest and $A=P(1+i)^{n}$ for compound interest, then compare the two amounts.

provenance.verifier_reason: I re-solved it myself. Bank A: 1450(1+0.11x3)=1450x1.33=R1928.50. Bank B: 1450x1.105^3=1956.387, which rounds to R1956.39. Both match the canonical solution, and Bank B is the answer. The refutation uses the book's own formulas A=P(1+in) and A=P(1+i)^n. Its description of simple versus compound interest matches the book's wording (interest on the principal only, versus interest on principal plus earlier interest). It argues against the error itself: rates alone cannot decide when the two accounts earn interest differently. It then gives the numbers that show it, rather than only restating the method. No step names a question id, page, figure or review history. The only remark beyond the book is that comparing rates works when both accounts earn interest the same way. That is a true, harmless concession, so I accept it. The error is real: Bank A is the book's own wrong option, and the 11% versus 10.5% rates invite exactly this shortcut. The signal is the standard fingerprint for this error.

misconceptions.label: Charges interest on the full cash price, deposit not taken off
misconceptions.description: The student uses the cash price as the starting amount $P$ in $A=P(1+in)$, forgetting that the deposit is paid up front and only the rest is borrowed.
misconceptions.signal: The accumulated amount or monthly repayment matches working from the full cash price, for example about 399.67 a month instead of 359.70 for a R4400 microwave with a 10% deposit, at 9% p.a. over 12 months.

refutation.text_md: You used the cash price as the amount being borrowed. That is an easy thing to do, because the cash price is the biggest number in the question. Your plan of using the simple interest formula and then dividing by the number of months is the right one; the slip is in the amount it starts from.

The deposit is paid in cash at the start, so that part of the price is never borrowed and no interest is charged on it. The amount borrowed, $P$, is only what is left: $P=\text{cash price}-\text{deposit}$, where the deposit is its percentage of the cash price.

See it in one case. A microwave has a cash price of R4400, with a 10% deposit and then 12 months at 9% p.a. The deposit is $4400\times\frac{10}{100}=440$, so $P=4400-440=3960$. Then $A=3960(1+0.09\times1)=4316.40$ and the monthly repayment is $\frac{4316.40}{12}=359.70$.
Starting from 4400 instead gives $A=4400(1+0.09\times1)=4796$, which is about R399.67 a month. That is too much, because it charges interest on the R440 that was already paid as the deposit.

So before you use $A=P(1+in)$, check for a deposit. Work out its percentage of the cash price, subtract it to get $P$, then find $A$ and divide by the number of months. If the question mentions no deposit, there is nothing to take off and $P$ is the cash price.

provenance.verifier_reason: I re-solved it. Deposit 4400 x 0.10 = 440, P = 3960, A = 3960 x 1.09 = 4316.40, monthly 4316.40/12 = 359.70. The wrong route gives 4400 x 1.09 = 4796, and 4796/12 = 399.67. These match ex9-3-1a, b and c. The error is supported by the worked example's own note that a new opening balance is needed because the deposit is paid in cash. The refutation argues against this slip rather than restating the method. It explains that the deposit is never borrowed, shows the contrast numerically, and gives the no-deposit case (P is the cash price), which matches ex9-3-4a. It names no question id, page, figure or review history. The signal figures are correct and describe a student who skipped the deposit.

misconceptions.label: Uses an interest-on-interest formula instead of simple interest
misconceptions.description: The student grows the loan with a formula in which interest is charged on earlier interest, instead of the simple interest formula $A=P(1+in)$ that a hire purchase agreement uses.

refutation.text_md: Some loans and savings do add interest on top of earlier interest, so it is natural to reach for that kind of formula here. The rest of your plan, finding the loan after any deposit and dividing the final amount by the number of months, is still the right one.

A hire purchase agreement is charged at simple interest, so the simple interest formula is the one to use every time: $A=P(1+in)$, where $i$ is the yearly rate as a decimal and $n$ is the number of years.

In simple interest, interest is charged only on the amount first borrowed, never on interest already added. Take a loan of R2250 at 7.5% p.a. over 2 years. Each year's interest is $2250\times0.075=168.75$, the same in year 2 as in year 1, so $A=2250+2\times168.75=2587.50$. This is exactly what $2250(1+0.075\times2)$ gives.

A formula that charges interest on interest would charge year 2's interest on more than R2250, so year 2 would cost more than year 1. The amount to pay back, and so the monthly repayment, would come out too large for what the agreement says.
So in any hire purchase question, find $P$ (the cash price less any deposit), write $A=P(1+in)$ with $n$ in years, and then divide $A$ by the number of months.

provenance.verifier_reason: The book states in a caution that hire purchase uses simple interest, so always use the simple interest formula. Several canonical solutions repeat this (we07, ex9-3-3b). The error of reaching for an interest-on-interest formula is the one that caution guards against. The refutation's example matches we07: R2250 at 7.5% for 2 years gives 168.75 a year, A = 2250 + 337.50 = 2587.50, and 2250 x 1.15 = 2587.50, so it is correct. It uses the book's own method and answer. It argues against this error by explaining that interest is charged only on the original amount, and that interest on interest would make year 2 cost more than year 1, so the repayment would be too large. It names no question id, page, figure or review history. The entry has no signal, so signal_ok is true.

misconceptions.label: Judges the cheaper deal by the smaller monthly payment
misconceptions.description: Asked which hire purchase offer costs the least interest, the student picks the offer with the smaller monthly payment without comparing what each offer costs in interest.
misconceptions.signal: Picks the offer with the smaller monthly payment as the one with the least interest.

refutation.text_md: You compared the monthly payments and chose the smaller one. That is a sensible instinct if you are thinking about what fits your monthly budget, but this question asks about the interest, and that depends on how much is paid altogether compared with the cash price.

Look at the totals. Store A collects $350\times24=8400$ and store B collects $175\times48=8400$. Both stores take the same R8400. Store B's payment is smaller only because the same amount is spread over 48 months instead of 24.

Interest is what is paid above the cash price, so we need each store's cash price. Use $A=P(1+in)$ with $A=8400$ and $i=0.075$, taking $n=2$ years for store A and $n=4$ years for store B: $8400=P(1+0.075\times2)$ for store A and $8400=P(1+0.075\times4)$ for store B. Then divide to find $P$ each time.

Store B's longer time makes the bracket $1+in$ bigger, so dividing the same R8400 by it gives a smaller cash price. The interest, $8400-P$, is then bigger. Store A has the larger cash price and so charges less interest, which makes store A the one to choose.
So for "least interest", never stop at the monthly payment. Find each offer's total paid, work back to its cash price with $A=P(1+in)$, and compare the interest, $A-P$, for each offer.

provenance.verifier_reason: Both stores total 350 x 24 = 8400 and 175 x 48 = 8400, so the claim in the refutation is correct. Working back correctly: A has 1+0.075x2 = 1.15 and B has 1+0.075x4 = 1.30. P is therefore smaller for B, so B's interest (8400 - P) is larger and store A is the right answer, as in the book. The refutation's qualitative reasoning (a bigger bracket gives a smaller cash price and so more interest) is valid and uses the book's method. It gives no intermediate numbers, so it does not repeat the book's printed slips (2.15 and 4.3 instead of 1.15 and 1.3), and the final answer A is unchanged. The error is supported by the question itself, where store B is the lower-payment option. It names no question id, page or review history. 'Store A' and 'store B' are visible on the question the option is attached to. The signal fits a student choosing B because its payment is lower.

misconceptions.label: Uses the rate as a whole number
misconceptions.description: The student puts the percentage into the bracket as it is written, such as $1+3$, instead of converting it to $\frac{3}{100}$ or $0.03$ first.
misconceptions.signal: The expected population comes out many times larger than the current population, far more than a yearly percentage rise could produce.

refutation.text_md: You have the formula, and the numbers are in the right places. What is missing is the conversion: a percentage means 'out of 100', so 16% is $\frac{16}{100}=0.16$, not 16.

See what $1+16$ does. It multiplies the population by 17 every year, so 1600 residents would become $1600\times 17=27\ 200$ after only one year of a 16% rise. But 16% of 1600 is 256, so after one year there are $1600+256=1856$ people, which is $1600\times 1.16$.
That is why the working converts first, for example $i=\frac{0.4}{100}=0.004$, and only then makes the bracket $1+0.004$. The bracket for a yearly growth rate is a number a little bigger than 1.
Before you substitute, turn the rate into $i$ by dividing by 100, then write $1+i$. If your bracket is 2 or more, such as $1+3$, the rate has not been converted yet.

provenance.verifier_reason: Real error, and the canonical solutions (ex9-5-3 with i=0.16, ex9-7-32 with i=0.4/100=0.004) show the conversion it skips. The arithmetic is correct. 1+16=17 gives 1600*17=27200. 16% of 1600 is 256, so 1856=1600*1.16. i=0.4/100=0.004, so the bracket is 1+0.004. The refutation targets the missing conversion and gives a concrete check (the bracket should be a little above 1). 'A bracket of 2 or more means not converted' is a sufficient test for every rate in this LO (all well below 100%), and the text does not claim the converse. The signal (an answer many times the current population) fits 1+3 over 6 years, which is about 4096 times, and no correct answer in this LO behaves that way.

misconceptions.label: Adds the same growth every year
misconceptions.description: The student treats population growth as adding the same amount every year, writing $P(1+i\times n)$ instead of multiplying by $(1+i)$ once for each year.

refutation.text_md: You have the right ingredients: the starting population, the rate as a decimal and the number of years. The slip is in how the years are used. Writing $P(1+i\times n)$ works out every year's growth on the starting population, as if the population never got bigger.
A population grows on what it is now, not on what it started as. Take 1600 residents growing at 16% a year. After one year there are $1600\times 1.16=1856$ people.

In the second year the 16% is taken of 1856, not of 1600: $\frac{16}{100}\times 1856=296.96$, which is more than the 256 that 16% of 1600 gives. After two years there are $1856+296.96=2152.96$ people.

Adding 16% of the starting 1600 twice, $1600(1+0.16\times 2)$, gives only 2112, so it under-counts. Multiplying by $(1+i)$ once for every year is what gives 2152.96, and that is exactly what the compound interest formula does: $1600(1+0.16)^{2}=2152.96$.
So keep $n$ as the raised number on the whole bracket: $A=P(1+i)^{n}$, never $P(1+i\times n)$. If you are unsure, check one year at a time as above.

provenance.verifier_reason: Real error for this LO: P(1+i*n) is the simple-interest shape applied where the canonical method is A=P(1+i)^n. I re-worked every number in the refutation. 1600*1.16=1856. 16% of 1856 is 296.96, versus 256 for 16% of 1600. 1856+296.96=2152.96. 1600(1+0.16*2)=2112. 1600(1.16)^2=2152.96, which agrees with the canonical ex9-5-3 intermediate value. The steps argue against the 'same growth each year' idea itself (growth is taken on the current population), not just the formula. No question ids, page numbers, figures or review history appear in the text. Minor note: it reuses the numbers of a book exercise, so it shows that exercise's intermediate value, but this is not a correctness or sourcing defect.

misconceptions.label: Swaps the rate and the number of years
misconceptions.description: The student puts the number of years in the rate position and the percentage in the raised number on the bracket, because both are just numbers in the question.

refutation.text_md: You have picked out the right numbers and you know the formula needs a bracket and a raised number. The only mix-up is which number goes where, because both are just numbers in the question.

Ask what each number counts. The percentage followed by p.a. is the growth in one year, so it belongs in the bracket as $i$. The number of years is how many times that growth is applied, so it is $n$, the raised number.

Take a rate of 0.7% p.a. over 12 years: $i=\frac{0.7}{100}$ and $n=12$, so the working is $\left(1+\frac{0.7}{100}\right)^{12}$. Swapped, it would read $\left(1+\frac{12}{100}\right)^{0.7}$, which describes 12% growth a year for only 0.7 of a year, a completely different situation.

Before you substitute, write down the known variables the way the worked examples do: $P$ is the starting population, $i$ is the percentage written as a decimal and $n$ is the number of years. Then copy each one into its own place in $A=P(1+i)^{n}$.

provenance.verifier_reason: Real, natural transposition error, since both quantities are just numbers in the question. The refutation is correct and uses the book's own data (0.7% over 12 years, as in the canonical ex9-5-2 solution): i=0.7/100, n=12, so (1+0.7/100)^12. The swapped form (1+12/100)^0.7 is correctly described as 12% a year for 0.7 of a year. It argues against the swap by asking what each number counts, and the variable list P, i (as a decimal), n matches the canonical solutions' 'known variables' step. The phrase 'the way the worked examples do' is generic and names no specific example, id or page.

misconceptions.label: Adds or subtracts amounts in different currencies without converting first
misconceptions.description: The student takes an amount in a foreign currency straight off an amount in rands, or adds it to one, as if both amounts were in the same currency.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the plain difference or sum of the two numbers, for example 49 000 from R50 000 and €1000.

refutation.text_md: You have the right idea about what happens: the gift reduces what Mathe still has to save. The slip is treating €1000 as if it were R1000.
Euros and rands are different currencies, so their numbers cannot be subtracted directly. With €1 = R13.22, one euro is worth R13.22, so €1000 is worth much more than R1000.
Taking $50\,000-1000=49\,000$ removes only R1000. First change the gift into rands: $1000\times 13.22=\text{R}13\,220$. Now both amounts are in rands, and $50\,000-13\,220=\text{R}36\,780$.
The same care applies when Kayla spends 65 000 MWK. Her R5000 has to become kwacha first: $5000\times 39.46=197\,300$ MWK. Only then can the spending come off: $197\,300-65\,000=132\,300$ MWK.

Before you add or subtract, convert every amount into the same currency using the exchange rate. Do the subtraction or addition in that one currency, and convert again only if the question asks for a different one.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and supported: ex9-6-6 invites 50000 - 1000 = 49000, and ex9-6-8 invites subtracting kwacha spending from a rand amount. The refutation follows the canonical method exactly: 1000 x 13.22 = R13 220, then 50 000 - 13 220 = R36 780. The Kayla step is also right: 5000 x 39.46 = 197 300 MWK, then minus 65 000 = 132 300 MWK. Both match the canonical solutions. It argues against the specific slip of treating euros as rands and gives a general rule (convert to one currency, then add or subtract), which the book uses. The only weakness is presentational: Mathe's R50 000 and Kayla's rate are not set up in the text. This does not affect correctness, and there is no id, page, figure or review reference.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies or divides by the exchange rate the wrong way round
misconceptions.description: The student uses the exchange rate in the right place but with the wrong operation, multiplying when the amount should be divided by the rate, or dividing when it should be multiplied.
misconceptions.signal: The converted amount is the wrong size for the rate, for example 106 800 euros from R10 000 when one euro costs R10.68.

refutation.text_md: You picked out the exchange rate and used it, and that is the right ingredient. The slip is in the operation: the rate was multiplied where it should divide, or divided where it should multiply.

A rate such as 1 euro = R10.68 says that one of the first currency is worth that many of the second. Start with an amount in the first currency (euros) and every euro brings R10.68, so you multiply by the rate. The median lies halfway between the two middle values: $\text{median}=\frac{11+14}{2}=12.5$. Here the median is not one of the values in the set, and that is fine.

Bread masses are continuous: a mass can be any real number, not just a few fixed values. When measurements can fall anywhere, two loaves matching exactly is usually a coincidence rather than a pattern, so a repeated value does not tell you which mass is typical. This is why the book says we can usually not compute the mode of a continuous data set.

Here is what goes wrong in practice. Among Monday's ten masses, $789.0\ \text{g}$ appears twice, so you might call it the mode. But it is the lightest mass of the day, well below Monday's mean of $800.8\ \text{g}$ and median of $801.8\ \text{g}$. Two loaves happening to match tells you nothing about where the typical loaf sits.

So for continuous data like these, do not report a mode. Write that the data are continuous, so the mode cannot be computed. Then work out the mean (add the ten masses and divide by $10$) and the median (sort the masses and take the value halfway between the two middle ones), and use those two to judge whether the loaves meet the requirement.

refutation.text_md: Part of this is right: the median hardly reacts to one extreme value. The slip is going from "hardly" to "not at all". The claim is that the median is less affected than the mean, not that it stays put.
See what adding one value does. With 10 learners the sorted list has an even number of values, so the median lies halfway between the fifth and sixth values: $\frac{156+157}{2}=156.5$ cm.

With the eleventh learner there are 11 values, an odd number, so the median is now the sixth value of the new sorted list, which is $157$ cm. The number of values changed, so the middle place moved, and the median moved with it.
The median changed by $0.5$ cm, while the mean changed by $2.3$ cm. That is small compared with the mean, but it is not zero.
To compare properly, sort the data again with the new value in it, find the middle of the new list, and write both medians and the change. Then say which measure moved less. Here it is the median.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is a plausible over-reading of the book's remark that the median is less affected by outliers. The canonical solution answers it directly: the median changes by only 0.5 cm, not by zero. The refutation is correct and consistent with the canonical method. With 10 values the median is (156+157)/2 = 156.5, the average of the fifth and sixth values. With 11 values it is the sixth value, 157. The changes of 0.5 for the median and 2.3 for the mean match the book. It argues against the specific slip, going from "hardly" to "not at all", rather than restating the method. It names no question id, page, figure or review history, and it introduces no measure or method the book lacks. The step 3 remark that the middle place moved is true here and is a mechanical reading of the book's own step. The signal (says the median is the same, or not affected at all) fits this error and would not misdiagnose a student who correctly says "less affected".

misconceptions.label: Puts the mode in the set, but not as the most frequent value
misconceptions.description: The student builds a data set with the right mean and median but includes the stated mode only once, or lets two other values repeat as often as it does, as if being in the set were enough to make a value the mode.
misconceptions.signal: A proposed data set in which the stated mode appears only once, or in which another value occurs as many times as the stated mode does.

refutation.text_md: Putting the age $2$ into your set is the right start, and your set may well have the right mean and median. But the mode is not just an age that appears in the set. It is the age that occurs most often.

Try a set with a single $2$, such as $\{1, 2, 3, 8, 11\}$. Its total is $1+2+3+8+11=25$, so the mean is $\frac{25}{5}=5$, and the middle value is $3$. But every age appears once, so nothing makes $2$ the age that occurs most often. The mode is not $2$.

The median is $3$, so $3$ sits in the third position of the ordered set. Every age after it is $3$ or more, so the only positions left for a $2$ are the first two. One $2$ is not enough for the mode to be $2$, so both of those positions must be $2$.
Take care with the last two ages as well. If $x_4$ and $x_5$ were the same age, that age would also occur twice, and then the mode would not be $2$.

So write the mode in twice: $\{2, 2, 3, x_4, x_5\}$. The mean then gives $2+2+3+x_4+x_5=25$, so $x_4+x_5=18$. Choose two different ages that add to $18$, for example $4$ and $14$, which gives $\{2, 2, 3, 4, 14\}$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and is the book's own warning in the five-ages worked example: one 2 is not enough, both x1 and x2 must be 2, and x4 and x5 must differ or the mode is not 2. I checked every step. The set {1,2,3,8,11} sums to 25 (mean 5, median 3, no repeated age). Ordering forces positions 4 and 5 to be 3 or more. {2,2,3,x4,x5} gives x4+x5=18. The example {2,2,3,4,14} is the book's Data set 1. The refutation argues against the error with a counterexample rather than restating the method. It names no question id, page, figure or review history, and it teaches nothing outside the book. One nit: it warns only about x4=x5, and the pair 3 and 15 would also tie with 2 (the book's prose lists that pair too). Nothing the refutation literally says is false, so I confirm. The signal is mathematically sound: a stated mode appearing once, or tied by another value, is exactly the error.

covers.text: No value repeats, so the set has no mode at all
Two or more values tie at the top, so the set has more than one mode

misconceptions.label: Puts a number at the edge of a range into the neighbouring range
misconceptions.description: The student sorts a value that sits at the edge of a range, such as a $4$ in ranges $0$–$3$ and $4$–$7$, into the next or previous range, so one column is counted one too many and its neighbour one too few.

refutation.text_md: You may have put a number that sits at the edge of a range into its neighbour, for example a $4$ into the range $0$–$3$. Going range by range through the sorted list is the right plan. The slip is only in where the edge numbers go.
Each range includes both numbers in its label, so $4$–$7$ holds $4$, $5$, $6$ and $7$. The next range starts at the very next whole number, so every whole number belongs to exactly one range.

Say the sorted values of a group of learners begin $1, 4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 8$, and the ranges are $0$–$3$ and $4$–$7$. The range $0$–$3$ has just the $1$, so its count is $1$. The range $4$–$7$ has the $4$ and the four $6$s, so its count is $5$. Slip the $4$ into $0$–$3$ and you would count $2$ and $4$ instead, and both columns would come out wrong.
To count a range, first write out the whole numbers it covers, for example $4, 5, 6, 7$. Then count every value in the sorted list that is one of those numbers. The edge numbers count.

provenance.verifier_reason: Edge values are real in the book's data. For example, 4, the 8s, the 12s and 16 sit at range edges in the first 'which column is wrong' item, and the canonical grouping puts each in exactly one inclusive range. The book's own stem '0 <= number <= 2' supports the claim that both ends of a label are included. I recomputed the worked example: sorted 1,4,6,6,6,6,8 gives 0-3 count 1 and 4-7 count 5, and slipping the 4 gives 2 and 4. That is correct and matches the book's grouping. The advice to write out the whole numbers in a range is a way of applying the book's group-and-count method, not a different method. There are no forbidden references. Option D on the playing-cards item is the one column where this slip lands cleanly. Moving the two 11s from 8-11 into 12-15 makes C come to 3, which matches the drawn column, and D come to 5 against the drawn 3. D is then the only column that disagrees, so the student picks D.

misconceptions.label: Skips a range that has no column
misconceptions.description: The student checks only the ranges that have a column drawn, so a range with no column, which the histogram shows as $0$ values, is never compared with the data.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to check the columns you can see. But a range with no column drawn above it is still a range on the graph, and the empty space is telling you something: there are $0$ values in that range.

So it has to be checked against the data like every other range. Say a range such as $16$–$19$ has no column, and the data holds $16, 17, 17, 18$ and $19$. That is $5$ values in the range, so the histogram says $0$ where the data says $5$.

That changes how to search. Once the columns that are drawn each agree with the count from the grouped data, none of them is the incorrect one, and the mistake is in a range you have not compared yet.

Next time, order the data, group it into every range along the bottom of the graph, and write each count beside its range, writing $0$ where there is no column. The range where the count and the column disagree is the incorrect one.

provenance.verifier_reason: The book's own item hinges on this: the empty 16-19 column is drawn as 0 when the data has 16,17,17,18,19, which is 5. I recomputed the other four columns (1, 5, 3, 6) and they all agree with the data, so the statement that none of the drawn columns is the wrong one is true. The refutation's example (16, 17, 17, 18, 19 gives 5 where the graph says 0) is correct. Writing 0 for an empty range and comparing every range follows the canonical order-group-compare method. There are no forbidden references and nothing is taught beyond the book.

misconceptions.label: Accepts a data set that matches only some of the ranges
misconceptions.description: The student takes a data set as the match once one or two of its ranges give the same counts as the columns, without grouping all of its values into every range.

refutation.text_md: You found a range where the data set and the histogram agree, and that part is real: the data set does have the right number of values there. What is missing is the rest, because agreeing in some ranges does not make a data set the match.
A data set matches a histogram only when every range gives the same count as its column, and a range with no column counts as $0$. One range that disagrees is enough to rule the data set out.

For example, take a data set with $3, 2, 1$ and $3$ in the range $0$–$3$. That is $4$ values, which agrees with a column $4$ tall over that range. But the same data set has $5, 5, 6, 5$ and $4$ in the range $4$–$7$: that is $5$ values, and the column over that range is only $4$ tall. The first range agreed and the second did not, so this data set is not the match.
So order each data set, group it into every range on the graph, and compare range by range. Cross a data set off the moment one range disagrees, and keep the one where every range agrees.

provenance.verifier_reason: I recomputed every data set against its histogram. Each attached option agrees with the drawn columns in some but not all ranges. The refutation's rule matches the canonical method: group each data set into every range, a range with no column counts as 0, and one disagreement rules the set out. Its example is arithmetically right (3,2,1,3 gives 4 in 0-3; 5,5,6,5,4 gives 5 in 4-7 against a column 4 high). It teaches nothing beyond the book and names no forbidden reference.

misconceptions.label: Reads a tall column as big numbers
misconceptions.description: The student takes the height of a column to say how large the values in that range are, instead of how many values fall in that range.

refutation.text_md: You are reading a tall column as meaning big numbers. That is a natural first guess, and you are right that the height tells you something about the values in that range. What it tells you is how many values are there, not how big they are.

The numbers under the columns, like $12$–$15$, say which values a range covers. The height of the column says how many of the values in the data set land in that range. A tall column is the range where most of the values are, whether those values are small or large.

For example, with $15$ learners counting their stones, a column over $12$–$15$ that is $6$ high means six learners have between $12$ and $15$ stones. It does not say that any of them has $6$ stones. All the column heights together add up to $15$, the number of learners, because each learner's value lands in exactly one column.
To count the values in a range, find its column and read its height. That number is your count.

provenance.verifier_reason: Real and common histogram error, and the book's caution (tall column = the range where most values lie) backs the correction. The refutation's example matches the book's 15-learner stones histogram: the 12-15 column is 6 high and the heights 1+4+1+3+6 sum to 15. It tells the student to read the column height as the count, which is the canonical method for the count-in-a-range questions. It names no question id, page, figure number or review history, and it teaches nothing beyond the book. The opening line 'you are right that the height tells you something' is loose but not wrong, since height does tell how many values are in the range.

misconceptions.label: Expects the grouped mean to be the exact mean
misconceptions.description: The student treats the answer from grouped data as the true mean of the original values, or is puzzled that it can differ from the mean of the individual values.

refutation.text_md: Your working can be spot on and still not give the exact mean, and that is fine. The number you get from grouped data is an **estimate** of the mean, not the exact mean of the original values.

Grouping loses information. Once a value is placed in a range, all we know is that it lies somewhere in that range. In the taxi data, 16 weeks had between $700$ and $800$ passengers. One of those weeks could be $701$, another $799$, and the groups cannot tell us which.

So the method treats every value in a group as lying at the centre of its range: all 16 of those weeks are counted as $750$. The book makes the same point: with grouped data the estimates of the centre change, because some information is lost.
Use the method as it stands. Multiply each group's centre by its count, add these up, and divide by the total count: $\frac{33600}{48}=700$. Then call it what it is, an estimate of the mean.

provenance.verifier_reason: I re-worked it from the histogram. The counts are 4, 6, 12, 16, 8 and 2, which total 48. The centres give 4(450)+6(550)+12(650)+16(750)+8(850)+2(950)=33600, and 33600/48=700. That matches canonical ex10-4-3b and ex10-4-3c. The error is real for this objective, which is an estimate of the mean of grouped data. Caution b03788 supports it: information is lost when values are placed in a range. The refutation argues against the error itself, that the grouped mean is the exact mean. It does not just restate the method. Its claims are mathematically right and stay inside the book: grouping loses information, every value is treated as sitting at the centre of its range, and the result is an estimate. It names no question id, page, numbered figure or review history. It uses the taxi data, which is the data the student sees in this objective's questions, and it states the numbers itself.

misconceptions.label: Looks for one most-common value instead of the modal group
misconceptions.description: The student expects the mode to be a single most common value, as with ungrouped data, and is unsure why the answer for grouped data is a range.

refutation.text_md: Looking for what occurs most often is the right idea for a mode. What changes with grouped data is what you are given: a count for each range, not the individual values.

Because the values have been placed in ranges, you cannot see which single number occurs most often. That information is gone. What the table or histogram does show is how many values fall in each range.

That is why we ask for the **modal group**: the group with the highest number of data values. The book notes that the grouped mode can be a better estimate of the mode than a single most common value, because the grouping shows the range in which the values are clustered.

In the taxi data the groups hold $4$, $6$, $12$, $16$, $8$ and $2$ values. The highest count is $16$, in the group $700<x\leq800$. The $16$ only tells you how many values lie in that group, so the modal group is the range itself.
To find a modal group: compare the counts, pick the largest, and write down the range it belongs to.

provenance.verifier_reason: The modal group is the group with the highest count. Here that is 16 in 700<x<=800, which matches canonical ex10-4-3a and the worked examples. The refutation states the six counts correctly and says the 16 is a count, so the answer is the range. Cautions b03792 and b03796 support it: the grouped mode shows where the values cluster, and the single-value mode is problematic for continuous data. The wording is hedged ('can be a better estimate') and does not go beyond the book. It argues against the 'one most common value' expectation and does not only restate the method. It contains no question id, page number, figure number or review history, and the numbers it uses are self-contained.

misconceptions.label: Expects removing one value to leave the range unchanged
misconceptions.description: When asked what happens to the range if the smallest or largest value is removed, or when a value that is not typical of the rest is present, the student expects the range to stay the same or hardly change, forgetting that the range is built only from the largest and the smallest values.
misconceptions.signal: After the smallest value has been removed, the student gives the original range again as the new range (for the worked set, 9 instead of 6), or says the range stays the same.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to think that taking away one number out of many should hardly change anything, and you are right that all the other values stay exactly as they were. The catch is that the range does not use all the values: it uses only the largest and the smallest.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest value. In the set $\{1, 4, 5, 8, 6, 7, 5, 6, 7, 4, 10, 9, 10\}$ the smallest value is $1$ and the largest value is $10$, so the range is $10-1=9$.

Now take the $1$ away. The smallest value left is $4$, so the range becomes $10-4=6$. Only one number was removed, yet the range dropped from $9$ to $6$, because the number removed was one of the two numbers the range is made from.
The book calls a value that is not typical of the other values an outlier, and the $1$ here is one. An outlier has a big influence on the range: the range is very sensitive to outliers.
So when you are asked what happens if a value is removed, cross it out, find the smallest and the largest values that are left, and subtract again. Here that gives $10-4=6$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and rests on the book's own remarks that the range is very sensitive to outliers and that a value not typical of the others has a big influence on the range. I re-solved the worked set: smallest 1 and largest 10 give 10-1=9. Removing the 1 makes the smallest 4, so 10-4=6. The refutation reaches both answers (9 and 6) and uses the book's method. It argues against the belief that the range stays put when one value goes, by pointing out that the range uses only the largest and smallest values. It names no question id, page, figure or review history, and teaches nothing beyond the book. The signal (the original range given again, 9 instead of 6, or 'the range stays the same') matches the error.

covers.text: The range stays at $21$, because only one of the values is removed.

misconceptions.label: Counts to the rank in the list as given, without sorting first
misconceptions.description: The student works out the rank with the percentile formula but counts along the data in the order it was printed, instead of first sorting the values from smallest to largest.
misconceptions.signal: Each answer is built from values at the right positions of the list as it was printed, so for a data set that is not already in order the median and quartiles come out wrong. For the twelve-value data set 3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50 this gives 4.5, 18.5 and 27 instead of 6.5, 18 and 29.

refutation.text_md: You worked out the rank correctly and then counted to that position, which is the right instinct. The slip is that a rank is a position in the data set **after it has been sorted** from smallest to largest, and the list you are given is usually in no particular order.

Take $\{3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50\}$. The rank of the lower quartile is $r=\frac{25}{100}(12-1)+1=3.75$, so it lies between the third and fourth values. Counting along the list as printed, those are $1$ and $8$, which gives $\frac{1+8}{2}=4.5$. But $1$ is the smallest number in the whole set, so it cannot be the third smallest.

The percentile formula only makes sense in sorted order. It gives rank $1$ for the minimum (the $0^{\text{th}}$ percentile) and rank $n$ for the maximum (the $100^{\text{th}}$ percentile). Those ranks only point to the smallest and largest values when the values are in order.

Sort first: $\{1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 12, 24, 25, 28, 30, 41, 50\}$. Now the third and fourth values are $5$ and $8$, and the lower quartile is $\frac{5+8}{2}=6.5$. Same rank, different values, different answer.
Make sorting your first step every time: rewrite the data from smallest to largest, check that you still have all $n$ values, and only then use the percentile formula and count along the sorted list.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real for this objective, which says to sort first. The worked example and both exercises with unsorted data open by ordering the data. I re-ran the arithmetic on the unsorted list 3, 5, 1, 8, 9, 12, 25, 28, 24, 30, 41, 50. Ranks 3.75, 6.5 and 9.25 point at 1 and 8, then 12 and 25, then 24 and 30, which gives 4.5, 18.5 and 27 as the signal says. The sorted list gives 6.5, 18 and 29, matching the canonical answer for the same data set. The refutation steps all check out: 1 cannot be the third smallest; the formula gives rank 1 for the minimum and rank n for the maximum; sorted, the third and fourth values are 5 and 8, so 6.5. It argues against this error with a concrete contradiction instead of restating the method. It takes the halfway value as the book does. The student-facing text contains no question id, page, figure or review history. The sorting advice stays within the book's method. The signal is specific and would not misfire on a correct student.

covers.text: The middle of the data as GIVEN, not the middle once it is sorted

misconceptions.label: Finds the middle of the data before putting it in order
misconceptions.description: The student finds the median and the quartiles by counting to the middle of the data in the order it is printed, instead of first writing the values from smallest to largest.

refutation.text_md: You are counting along the list to find the middle, and finding a quartile by its position is the right idea. The slip is doing that counting on the data in the order it was printed.

A quartile is the 25th, 50th or 75th percentile, and the rank from the percentile formula counts places in the ordered list. With 12 values the 25th percentile has rank $3.75$, which means between the third and fourth smallest values. In a list that is not in order, the third and fourth entries are just whatever happened to be written there.

See it go wrong with 15 timings printed in this order: $121, 137, 131, 135, 130, 128, 130, 126, 132, 127, 129, 120, 118, 125, 134$. The ranks are $4.5$ and $11.5$. In the printed order, the lower-quartile places hold $135$ and $130$, while the upper-quartile places hold $129$ and $120$. The "upper" quartile comes out smaller than the "lower" one, so $Q_3-Q_1$ would be negative. The upper quartile can never sit below the lower quartile, so that result tells you the data was not in order.

Before you count anything, write all the values in order from smallest to largest. Then use the percentile formula for the ranks, read $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ from that ordered list, and subtract: $Q_3-Q_1$. For the semi-interquartile range, halve that result. Those same 15 timings, put in order first, give an interquartile range of $6$.

provenance.verifier_reason: I worked every number myself. With n=12 the book's percentile formula gives rank 3.75, between the 3rd and 4th values, as the book does. For the 15 timings, n=15 gives ranks 0.25*14+1=4.5 and 0.75*14+1=11.5. In the printed order, positions 4 and 5 hold 135 and 130, so Q1 would be 132.5. Positions 11 and 12 hold 129 and 120, so Q3 would be 124.5. That gives Q3-Q1=-8, which is negative, so the counterexample is real and the refutation's description of it is accurate. Sorted, the list is 118,120,121,125,126,127,128,129,130,130,131,132,134,135,137. Q1=(125+126)/2=125.5, Q3=(131+132)/2=131.5, and the IQR is 6, matching the canonical answer. I also checked the canonical answers for ex10-5-6e (7, 6.5, 5), ex10-5-6f (3.5, 3.25, 2.5) and the untrained set in ex10-7-22b (Q1=139.5, Q3=148.5, IQR 9). All agree with the percentile-rank-on-ordered-data method used in the refutation, so there is no contradiction. The error is real for this objective because ex10-7-22b hands the student 15 unsorted values, while the book's worked example begins from an ordered data set. The refutation argues against the specific slip: it shows the counting going wrong with a concrete negative result, and then gives the corrected route and the semi-interquartile halving step. It names no question id, page, figure, reviewer or review history. Two minor points against it, neither of which changes the verdict: the line that a negative result tells you the data was not in order slightly over-claims, since a negative could also come from subtracting the wrong way round. The Q3 >= Q1 sanity check is an elementary consequence of the definitions, not something the book states, though it is correct. The refutation also states the answer 6 for the same data as ex10-7-22b, which is harmless once the student has already answered.

misconceptions.label: Reads the five numbers off the list as it was written, without ordering it first
misconceptions.description: The student counts to the middle, the quarter and the three-quarter positions (and may take the first and last values as the minimum and maximum) in the data as it was GIVEN, instead of first putting the values in order from smallest to largest.
misconceptions.signal: The median, or the average of the two middle values, is simply whatever sits in the middle of the list as it was written; the "minimum" and "maximum" are the first and last numbers written; or the five numbers do not increase from left to right (a first quartile larger than the median, say).

refutation.text_md: You counted to the middle of the list, and counting by position is the right idea: with 9 values the median is the 5th value, the first quartile is the 3rd and the third quartile is the 7th. What is missing is a step that comes before the counting: putting the data in order.

Position only means something once the values are lined up from smallest to largest. The median is the value with as many values below it as above it. The middle of a list that is still jumbled is just whichever number happened to be written there.

Try it on the florist's bouquets: $16, 14, 8, 12, 6, 5, 3, 5, 7$. The 5th value as written is $6$. But only three values are below $6$ (the $5$, $3$ and $5$) and five are above it, so $6$ is not in the middle. Put the data in order first: $3, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14, 16$. Now the 5th value is $7$, with four values below it and four above it. The median is $7$, not $6$.

The same trap catches the other three numbers. Read off the unordered list, the first value $16$ would be the "minimum" and the last value $7$ the "maximum", yet $3$ is in the list. The 3rd and 7th values as written, $8$ and $3$, would make the first quartile bigger than the third quartile. A five number summary has to increase from minimum to maximum, and that only happens once the data is ordered.

So make ordering your first line of working every time: write the data from smallest to largest. Then the minimum is the first value and the maximum is the last. Count along the ordered list for the median and the quartiles. With an even number of values, the median lies between the two middle values, so you take their average.

provenance.verifier_reason: Worked through every number myself. The book's first step is to order the data, and the exercise data (16, 14, 8, 12, 6, 5, 3, 5, 7) is given unsorted, so skipping that step is a real error for this objective. Canonical ordered list: 3, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 14, 16, with median 7 (5th of 9), Q1 5 (3rd) and Q3 12 (7th). The refutation matches this throughout. Positions for 9 values (5th, 3rd, 7th) match the canonical. The unordered 5th value is 6, with three values below it (5, 3, 5) and five above (16, 14, 8, 12, 7); ordered, 7 has four below and four above. The unordered first and last values (16 and 7) would give a wrong minimum and maximum, since 3 and 16 are in the list. The unordered 3rd and 7th values (8 and 3) would put Q1 above Q3. The closing remark that an even count means averaging the two middle values for the median matches the book's 12-value example, whose figure I checked (median 3.65, Q1 2.5, Q3 4.775). The method is the book's own and the refutation argues against this specific error rather than restating the method. No question id, page number, figure reference or review history appears in the label, description, signal or refutation steps. The florist data is quoted in full, so it is self-contained. The signal is diagnostic: a middle taken from the written order, first and last values taken as minimum and maximum, or non-increasing five numbers. The evidence field is empty, but the canonical's first step and the unsorted question data support the error. The cited distractors D0 and D1 were not shown to me, so I did not rely on them.

misconceptions.label: Takes the line inside the box for an end of the box
misconceptions.description: The student treats the line inside the box as the first or third quartile, instead of seeing that the quartiles are the two ends of the box and the line inside is the median.

refutation.text_md: It looks like you took the number to be a quartile. That is a sensible place to look, because the box is where the quartiles live. The catch is which part of the box: a box has three vertical lines, and they do three different jobs.
The book says the box shows the interquartile range, the distance between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$. So the two ends of the box are the quartiles. The line inside the box is the one that shows the median.

Try it on a plot whose whiskers reach $15$ and $35$ and whose box runs from $22$ to $28$, with a line inside the box at $25$. The two ends of the box give $Q_1 = 22$ and $Q_3 = 28$, and the line inside gives the median, $25$. If the line at $25$ were a quartile, the median would be left with no mark on the plot at all.

misconceptions.label: Names the sides from the wrong angle
misconceptions.description: The student labels opposite and adjacent from the other angle of the right-angled triangle (for example the angle at the ground when the angle with the wall is wanted), so the ratio chosen, and the angle found, belong to a different angle from the one asked for.

refutation.text_md: Naming the sides is the right first move, and you did it. The slip is that you named them from the other angle: "opposite" and "adjacent" depend on which angle you are looking from, so the ratio you wrote belongs to a different angle from the one the question asks for.

Then label from it: the opposite side is across from $x$, the adjacent side touches $x$ (and is not the hypotenuse), and the hypotenuse is across from the right angle. Choose the ratio that uses the two sides you know, such as $\sin x=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, and find $x$ on your calculator.

misconceptions.label: Stopping at one part of the height
misconceptions.description: The student finds the side of one right-angled triangle from the angle and gives it as the whole height or distance, when the height the question needs is made of two parts.

refutation.text_md: Your tangent step is sound: the angle really does give you a right-angled triangle and one of its sides. What has slipped is that this triangle covers only part of the height the question asks for.

An angle of elevation or of depression is measured from the horizontal at the observer. The triangle it makes therefore reaches only from that horizontal to the point being looked at, and not necessarily the whole way from the ground to the top.

Take someone on top of a block of flats, $200$ m from a cellphone tower. They look up at an angle of elevation of $34^\circ$ to the top of the tower and down at an angle of depression of $62^\circ$ to its bottom. The $34^\circ$ triangle gives only the part of the tower above their level: $200 \times \tan 34^\circ \approx 135$ m. The $62^\circ$ triangle gives only the part below it: $200 \times \tan 62^\circ \approx 376$ m. Giving $135$ m or $376$ m as the height of the tower leaves the other part out.

A lighthouse standing on a cliff works the same way. The angle of elevation to the top of the lighthouse is taken from the boat at sea level, so the vertical side of the triangle is the lighthouse plus the cliff: $10 + 75 = 85$ m. Working from $75$ m or $10$ m alone leaves out part of it.

Next time, ask which point the angle is aimed at, and mark the whole vertical side from the horizontal at the observer up or down to that point. If the figure shows more than one piece, add them: either find each piece with its own triangle and add, as in $135 + 376 = 511$ m, or add the pieces first and then use the tangent, as in $85$ m for the lighthouse.

misconceptions.label: Writing the ratio the wrong way up
misconceptions.description: The student finds the right two sides for the angle but writes the tangent ratio upside down, with the side beside the angle on top and the side across from it underneath, so the answer is divided by tan where it should be multiplied, or the other way round.

The $200$ m runs beside the $62^\circ$ angle (adjacent) and the drop to the foot of the tower is across from it (opposite). So $\tan 62^\circ = \dfrac{\text{drop}}{200}$ and $\text{drop} = 200 \times \tan 62^\circ \approx 376$ m.

Written upside down, $\tan 62^\circ = \dfrac{200}{\text{drop}}$ turns into $\text{drop} = 200 \div \tan 62^\circ \approx 106$ m. That is a very different answer, and it comes from treating the $200$ m as the side across from the angle when it is the side beside it.

Next time, mark the angle, label the opposite and adjacent sides from that angle, and write $\tan = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ before you put any numbers in. If the unknown is the opposite side you multiply, as in $x = 70\tan 38^\circ$. If the unknown is the adjacent side you divide, as in $x = \dfrac{8}{\tan 45^\circ}$.

misconceptions.label: Using the slanted side as the height
misconceptions.description: The student puts the length of a slanted side into the area formula as the height of a trapezium or parallelogram, instead of finding the dashed height that meets the base at a right angle.

refutation.text_md: You used the slanted side as the height. That is an understandable choice: it is a number printed on the shape, and the area formula really does need a height. The catch is that the height is the dashed line, which meets the bottom edge at a right angle. The slanted side leans over, so it is a different length.

Look at the right-angled triangle on the left of the shape. Its three sides are the slanted side, the dashed height and the piece of the bottom edge up to the dashed line. The slanted side is opposite the right angle, which makes it the longest side of that triangle. So the slanted side is always longer than the height, and putting it into the formula makes the height too big.

The book finds the height first, with the theorem of Pythagoras. For the trapezium with a 15 cm slanted side and a 9 cm piece of the bottom edge: $h^{2}=15^{2}-9^{2}=144$, so $h=12$. The height is 12 cm, which is shorter than the 15 cm side you were about to use.

Now the 12 goes into the area formula: $A=\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\frac{1}{2}(46)(12)=276\text{ cm}^{2}$. The same order works for the parallelogram with a 14 cm slanted side and an 8 cm piece of the bottom edge: $h^{2}=14^{2}-8^{2}$ gives the height, and only then do you use $A=b\times h$.

The move to use: if the shape shows a slanted side and a dashed line, but no number on the dashed line, do not use the slanted side as the height. Build the right-angled triangle, use $h^{2}=(\text{slanted side})^{2}-(\text{piece of the base})^{2}$ to find $h$, and then put $h$ into the area formula.

misconceptions.label: Base left out of the total surface area
misconceptions.description: The student adds up only the triangular sides of the pyramid and forgets that the base is part of the surface too.

refutation.text_md: You found the area of the triangular sides and stopped there, as if the surface of a pyramid were only the slanted faces you see from the side. That is a natural picture, and the sides are the harder part, so that part of your work counts.
But the total surface area is every face on the outside of the solid, and the base is one of those faces. The book's method has two parts: the area of the base, plus the area of the sides.

The base adds $7^{2}=49$. The total is $49+140=189$ square units, which is the same as $b(b+2h_s)=7(7+2(10))=189$. Stopping at 140 would leave 49 square units of the surface uncounted.

Before you finish, check that your working has both parts. Write the base area first ($b^{2}$ for a square base), then the area of the sides, and add them: $\text{total}=\text{area of base}+\text{area of sides}$.

misconceptions.label: Triangle area without the one half

The area of a triangle is $\frac{1}{2}bh$, and the book keeps the half in every triangular side, as in $4\left(\frac{1}{2}bh_s\right)$. Without the half you have found $bh_s$, which is twice the area of the triangle.

misconceptions.label: Vertical height used for the triangular sides
