misconceptions.label: Uses the vertical height instead of the slant height
misconceptions.description: The student puts the vertical height of the cone into the walls' formula $\pi r\times$ height, instead of the slant height measured along the side of the cone.
misconceptions.signal: The total is $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{vertical height})$, so it comes out smaller than the correct total.

refutation.text_md: You have the right plan: $\pi r^2$ for the base and $\pi r\times(\text{height})$ for the walls. The slip is which height. You used the vertical height, straight down from the top of the cone to the centre of the base. The walls slope, so the book measures them along the slant height, from the top down the side of the cone to the edge of the base.

The vertical height, the radius and the slant height make a right-angled triangle. The vertical height and the radius are the two shorter sides, meeting at the right angle at the centre of the base, and the slant height is the longest side. So the slant height is always longer than the vertical height, and using the vertical height makes the walls too small.

The book's cone with radius 4 and vertical height 14 shows how this works. The book first finds the slant height with the theorem of Pythagoras: $\sqrt{4^2 + 14^2} = \sqrt{212} = 2\sqrt{53}$. The walls are then $\pi\times 4\times 2\sqrt{53} = 8\pi\sqrt{53}$ and the total is $16\pi + 8\pi\sqrt{53} = 233.2\ \text{cm}^2$. Using 14 for the walls would give $16\pi + 56\pi = 72\pi$, about $226.2$, which is too small.

When a question gives both heights, as in the book's cone with radius 4, vertical height 9.16 and slant height 10, the walls use the slant height $10$. When only the vertical height is given, find the slant height first with $\sqrt{r^2 + (\text{vertical height})^2}$. Then use $\pi r^2 + \pi r\times(\text{slant height})$.

provenance.verifier_reason: All the maths checks against the figures and canonical solutions. For r=4 and vertical height 14, the slant height is sqrt(212) = 2 sqrt 53, the walls are 8 pi sqrt 53 and the total is 233.2 cm^2. Using 14 gives 16pi + 56pi = 72pi, about 226.2, which is smaller. The right triangle with the vertical height and radius as legs and the slant height as hypotenuse is correct, so the slant height is the longest side. The case where both heights are given (r=4, vertical height 9.16, slant height 10) uses the slant height 10, as the canonical solution does. The advice to find the slant height from sqrt(r^2 + h^2) when only the vertical height is given matches the worked example. It argues against this specific error and has no forbidden references.

misconceptions.label: Whole sphere's volume used for a half sphere
misconceptions.description: The student puts the full sphere volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ in for a solid that is only half a sphere, such as a half scoop of ice-cream, and never halves it.
misconceptions.signal: A half-sphere volume that is exactly double the correct one, for example 113.1 cm³ for a half scoop of radius 3 cm instead of 56.5 cm³.

refutation.text_md: You used the formula for a whole sphere, $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, and that part is right: it is the sphere formula. The catch is that this solid is only half a sphere, so the formula gives you twice the volume you need.

Take a half scoop of ice-cream with radius $3$ cm. A whole sphere of radius $3$ cm has volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3=36\pi\approx 113.1$ cm$^3$. The book's working says the volume of a half sphere is half the volume of a sphere, so the half scoop is only half of that.
So the scoop is $\frac{4}{3}\pi(3)^3\times\frac{1}{2}=18\pi\approx 56.5$ cm$^3$, not $113.1$ cm$^3$.

See what the doubling does to the comparison. The cone with radius $3$ cm and height $12$ cm holds $\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(12)=36\pi\approx 113.1$ cm$^3$. With the whole sphere's $113.1$ cm$^3$ the ice-cream would look exactly as big as the cone. The real scoop is $56.5$ cm$^3$, which is less than $113.1$ cm$^3$, so the melted ice-cream fits.
Next time you meet a half sphere, write $V=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\times\frac{1}{2}$, the whole-sphere formula times one half, then substitute $r$ and calculate.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and supported. The book's ice-cream question uses a half scoop and says its volume is half the volume of a sphere, and the half-sphere teaching item uses V=(4/3)πr³×1/2. The refutation's numbers all match the canonical solution: the whole sphere with r=3 gives (4/3)π·27=36π≈113.1; the half scoop is 18π≈56.5; the cone (1/3)π·9·12=36π≈113.1. The comparison step is also correct. The doubled value would equal the cone's volume, while the true scoop of 56.5 is less than 113.1, so the ice-cream fits, which is the book's conclusion (A: Yes). It does not wrongly claim the doubled value would flip the answer. The method is the book's (sphere formula times 1/2). The refutation argues against the specific slip (using the whole-sphere formula for a hemisphere) and does not merely restate the method. The wording 'the book's working' is a general mention and not a question id, page, figure number or review reference. The signal (exactly double, 113.1 vs 56.5) is accurate and specific to this error.

misconceptions.label: Slant height used as the height
misconceptions.description: The student puts the slant height (the length along the slanting side of the cone or pyramid) into the volume formula where the vertical height $H$ belongs.
misconceptions.signal: The volume comes out too big, because a slanting length is longer than the straight-up height. For example, a square pyramid with base side 8 units, vertical height 8 units and slant height 8.94 units gives 190.72 instead of 170.67.

refutation.text_md: You have the right formula and you have put in a real length from the question, which is good. The slip is which length. The slant height runs down along the side of the cone or pyramid, but the formula needs the vertical height $H$: the length that goes straight up from the base to the top.
The slant height leans over, so it is always longer than the vertical height. Using it makes the solid look taller than it really is, so the volume comes out too big.

Take a square pyramid with base side 8 units, vertical height $H=8$ units and slant height 8.94 units. With the vertical height, $V=\frac{1}{3}b^{2}H=\frac{1}{3}(8)^{2}(8)=\frac{512}{3}\approx 170.67$ units$^3$. Putting in 8.94 instead gives $\frac{1}{3}(8)^{2}(8.94)=190.72$ units$^3$, which is too big.

Sometimes the question gives the slant height and no vertical height. Then the radius, the vertical height and the slant height make a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the longest side, and Pythagoras gives $H$. For a cone with radius 5 cm and slant height 13 cm: $H^{2}=13^{2}-5^{2}=144$, so $H=12$ cm, and $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi(5)^{2}(12)=100\pi\approx 314.2$ cm$^3$.

Next time, before you substitute, ask which length goes straight up from the base. If the question gives it as $H$, use it and leave the slant height unused. If it is missing, find it with Pythagoras first, then put $H$ into the formula.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real here: the book's cone and pyramid questions deliberately give a slant height (7.28, 8.94, 8.60, 8.73) alongside H and then ignore it, and two questions (13 cm/5 cm cone, 20 cm/12 cm cone) require Pythagoras to turn the slant height into H. I checked the figures. 8.94, 7.28, 8.60 and 8.73 are the slant lengths along the face or side, and the vertical H is the dashed perpendicular. All the arithmetic in the refutation is correct: (1/3)(64)(8)=512/3≈170.67; (1/3)(64)(8.94)=190.72, which is too big; 13²−5²=144 so H=12, and V=100π≈314.2. These match the canonical answers. The method is the book's own (V=(1/3)b²H, cone V=(1/3)πr²H, H found by Pythagoras). The claim that the slant height is longer than H is true, since it is the hypotenuse. The refutation argues against the specific slip and does not just restate the method. It names no question id, page number, figure number or review history. The signal (volume too big, 190.72 vs 170.67) is accurate.

misconceptions.label: Counts the faces where the two solids meet
misconceptions.description: The student finds the full surface area of each solid and adds them, so the face the pyramid sits on and the pyramid's own base are counted even though both are covered.
misconceptions.signal: A total surface area larger than the exposed-faces total by the area of the face where the solids meet, or by twice that area.

refutation.text_md: You found the full surface area of each solid and added the two totals. Finding each solid's area is the right start, and so is adding. The catch is that two of the faces you counted are not on the outside of the finished solid.

Where the pyramid sits on the cube or prism, the pyramid's base is covered by the solid beneath it, and the face it sits on is covered by the pyramid. Nobody can see or touch either face, so neither is an exposed face, and the total surface area counts only the exposed faces.

Try a cube of side $5$ $\text{cm}$ with a square pyramid on top. Counting everything gives the cube's six faces, $6\times25=150$, plus the pyramid's base, $25$, plus its four triangles, $65$: that is $240$ $\text{cm}^2$. Counting only the exposed faces gives five faces of the cube, $5\times25=125$, plus the four triangles, $65$: that is $190$ $\text{cm}^2$. The extra $50$ $\text{cm}^2$ is exactly the two covered faces, $25$ each.

So before you add, ask which faces are covered. For the solid underneath, count every face except the one the pyramid sits on. For the pyramid, count only its slanted triangular faces and leave out its base. Then add the areas of those exposed faces.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real here. The book's worked example (cube with a square pyramid) states that one cube face and the pyramid's base are covered, so only 5 cube faces and 4 triangles count. Its worked example with the triangular prism also uses only the prism base, the prism sides and the exposed pyramid faces. I re-checked the refutation's numbers: 6x25=150, plus 25, plus 65 gives 240; 5x25=125 plus 65 gives 190; the difference is 50, which is two covered faces of 25 each. The 190 total matches the book's answer for the 5 cm cube with the 6 cm pyramid, and the 65 is 4 x 16.25 from slant height 6.5. The steps contain no question ids, page numbers, figure references or review history. The method taught (exclude the covered face and the pyramid's base, add the exposed faces) is the canonical one. The refutation argues against the specific mistake rather than just restating the method. The signal (total too large by one or two covered-face areas) would not misdiagnose a student. Minor weakness: the 65 for the triangles is not derived in the text, but it is correct.

misconceptions.label: Uses the whole height of the solid as the pyramid's height
misconceptions.description: Given the overall height of the composite solid, the student puts that number in as the height of the pyramid instead of subtracting the height of the cube or prism underneath it.

refutation.text_md: You used the height given for the whole solid as the height of the pyramid. The formula you chose, $\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base}\times H$, is the right one for the pyramid. What needs another look is the number you put in for $H$.

The height of the pyramid is measured from its base up to its tip, and the pyramid is only the top part of the solid. The overall height starts at the bottom of the whole solid, so it also includes the height of the cube or prism underneath.

Take a cube of side $7$ $\text{cm}$ with a square pyramid on top, and the whole solid is $22$ $\text{cm}$ tall. The pyramid's height is $22-7=15$ $\text{cm}$, so its volume is $\frac{1}{3}(7)^2(15)=245$ $\text{cm}^3$, and with the cube the total is $343+245=588$ $\text{cm}^3$. Using $22$ instead gives about $359.3$ $\text{cm}^3$ for the pyramid, which counts the cube's $7$ $\text{cm}$ of height a second time.

So subtract first: height of the pyramid $=$ overall height $-$ height of the cube or prism. Use that height in $\frac{1}{3}\times\text{base}\times H$, and in the theorem of Pythagoras if you need the slant height, then add the volumes.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and well supported. In the book's cube-and-pyramid examples the overall height is given (11 cm with a 5 cm cube; 22 cm with a 7 cm cube), and the pyramid's height must be found by subtraction (6 and 15 cm). I re-checked the refutation's arithmetic: pyramid height 22-7=15; (1/3)(49)(15)=245; 343+245=588, which matches the canonical answer 588; (1/3)(49)(22)=359.33, so 'about 359.3' is right. It uses the book's own formula and method, mentions Pythagoras only generically for the slant height, and cites no question id, page, figure or review history. It argues against the specific mistake of using the whole height, not just the method. It has no signal, so there is nothing to misdiagnose.

misconceptions.label: Uses the vertical height where the slant height belongs
misconceptions.description: The student puts the vertical height of the cone or pyramid straight into the surface area formula in place of the slant height, so the sloping surface is measured with a length that is too short.
misconceptions.signal: For a cone with radius 3 cm and vertical height 10 cm, the answer comes out as about $122.52\text{ cm}^2$ (that is $39\pi$) instead of $126.67\text{ cm}^2$.

refutation.text_md: You put the vertical height (the length that goes straight up through the middle of the solid) into the surface area formula where the slant height belongs. Your formula is the right one, and both lengths are called a height, so it is an easy swap to make.

They are different lengths. The vertical height runs straight up inside the solid, from the middle of the base to the top. The slant height runs along the sloping surface, from the top down to the edge of the base. Together with the radius of the base they make a right-angled triangle, and the slant height is its longest side, so it is always longer than the vertical height.

Take a cone with radius $3\text{ cm}$ and vertical height $10\text{ cm}$. Using $10$ as the slant height gives $\pi(3)(3+10)=39\pi\approx 122.52\text{ cm}^2$. The real slant height is $h_s=\sqrt{3^2+10^2}=\sqrt{109}\approx 10.44\text{ cm}$, and $\pi(3)(3+\sqrt{109})\approx 126.67\text{ cm}^2$. The first answer is too small because the surface slopes for $10.44\text{ cm}$, not $10\text{ cm}$.

A square pyramid works the same way, with one thing to watch. The vertical height lands in the middle of the base, so the other short side of the right-angled triangle is half of the base side, not the whole side. For a base side of $15\text{ cm}$ that short side is $7.5\text{ cm}$, and you use $h_s^2=(7.5)^2+h^2$.

So first ask what the length you were given is. If it is marked along the sloping side, it already is the slant height and you can use it straight away. If it is the vertical height, find the slant height first with the theorem of Pythagoras ($h_s^2=r^2+h^2$ for a cone), then put $h_s$ into the surface area formula: $\pi r(r+h_s)$ for a cone, or $b(b+2h_s)$ for a square pyramid, where $b$ is the whole base side.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real for this objective and supported by the canonical solutions. In the worked cone example the book finds the slant height first, with h_s = sqrt(3^2+10^2) = sqrt(109), and only then uses pi*r*(r+h_s) = 126.67 cm^2. The cone figure confirms r = 3 and a dashed vertical height of 10. The refutation's numbers check out: pi*3*(3+10) = 39*pi = 122.52, and sqrt(109) = 10.44, giving 126.67. The square-pyramid step matches the book's method too. The figure shows a 15 cm base and a 12 cm vertical height, the book uses (7.5)^2 + 12^2 for the slant height, and b(b+2h_s) is the book's formula with b the whole base side. The advice 'if marked along the sloping side, use it directly' agrees with the book's other cone example, where 20 cm along the slope goes straight into the surface-area formula. The refutation argues against the swap itself, giving the geometric reason (the slant height is the hypotenuse) and a numeric contrast, rather than just restating the method. It teaches only Pythagoras, the book's own tool. The label, description, signal and steps cite no question ids, pages, figures or review history. One side note for whoever owns the canonical: the book's final pyramid figure of 437.26 does not match its own formula, which gives about 649.5. The refutation never states a pyramid area, so it does not conflict with it.

misconceptions.label: Scales the whole surface area by one factor
misconceptions.description: When the radius of a cylinder is multiplied by $k$, the student multiplies the whole surface area by a single factor, $k$ or $k^2$, instead of finding how each term of the area formula changes.
misconceptions.signal: The new surface area of a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ is given as $kA$ or $k^2A$.

refutation.text_md: Scaling the area as one block is a natural move, because the volume really does change by a single factor ($k^2V$ when the radius is multiplied by $k$). The surface area is not like that: it is a sum of terms, and they do not all change by the same factor.
Start from $A=\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ and put in the new radius $kr$, leaving $h$ alone: $A_n=\pi(kr)^2+2\pi(kr)h=\pi k^2r^2+2\pi krh$.
Now look at the $k$'s one term at a time. The first term has $k^2$, because $r$ is squared in it. The second has only $k$, because $r$ appears once in it. So $A_n=k^2(\pi r^2)+k(2\pi rh)$.

No single factor can match this. With $k=2$ the first term is multiplied by 4 and the second by 2. Multiplying the whole area by 4 would make the second term twice what it should be, and multiplying the whole area by 2 would make the first term half what it should be.
So put the new dimension into every term of the area formula, then collect the $k$'s term by term. Don't try to attach one factor to the whole area.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and is supported by we20. The canonical A_n = k^2(pi r^2) + k(2 pi r h) is a term-by-term result with different factors, so a single factor k or k^2 on the whole area is a genuine wrong move. The refutation follows the canonical steps exactly: it starts from A = pi r^2 + 2 pi r h, substitutes kr, and collects k^2 on the first term and k on the second. The k=2 check is correct. Multiplying the whole area by 4 would double the second term, and multiplying it by 2 would halve the first. Step 1 correctly says the volume does scale by one factor, k^2 V. It cites no question id, page, figure or review history, and the signal (kA or k^2 A) is accurate. No options or predicates are attached. One note for upstream: the canonical formula A = pi r^2 + 2 pi r h has only one end disk, while the we20 figure shows a closed cylinder, which would give 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h. The refutation is faithful to the canonical solution, which is the authority, and its conclusion holds either way, so I am confirming it.

misconceptions.label: Volume grows by only $k$ when the radius is scaled
misconceptions.description: The student expects the volume to be multiplied by $k$ whenever any one dimension is multiplied by $k$, so for a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ they write $kV$ instead of $k^2V$, often by turning $\pi(kr)^2$ into $\pi kr^2$.
misconceptions.signal: The new volume of a cylinder whose radius is multiplied by $k$ is given as $kV$ (or $\pi kr^2h$) rather than $k^2V$.

refutation.text_md: You have spotted something true: when the height of a prism is multiplied by $k$, the volume is multiplied by $k$ too, because the new volume is $l\times b\times(kh)=kV$. The slip is carrying that pattern over to the radius, where it does not hold.

The height works that way because it appears in the volume formula once, as a single factor. The radius is different. In $V=\pi r^2\times h$ it appears squared, so the new radius $kr$ has to go in as $(kr)^2$.
The square applies to the whole of $kr$, not just to $r$: $(kr)^2=kr\times kr=k^2r^2$. Writing $\pi kr^2$ leaves out one of the two factors of $k$.
So the new volume is $V_n=\pi(kr)^2\times h=\pi k^2r^2\times h=k^2\times\pi r^2h=k^2V$. With $k=2$, doubling the radius makes the volume 4 times as big, not 2 times.

Next time, write the new dimension in brackets, for example $(kr)$, and put it into the original formula exactly where the old one stood. Expand the brackets, then group what is left as the original volume $V$. The factor in front of $V$ is your answer.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real for this objective. we19 shows the height scaling the volume by k, and a student can wrongly carry that over to the radius in we20, writing pi*k*r^2*h for pi*(kr)^2*h. Every step of the refutation checks out against we20: (kr)^2 = k^2 r^2, V_n = pi(kr)^2 h = k^2 V, and the k=2 case gives 4 times the volume. Step 1 matches we19's l*b*(kh) = kV. The argument is aimed at this slip, namely the single-factor pattern and the unsquared k, not just a restatement of the method. It uses no different method and teaches nothing outside the book. It cites no question id, page, figure or review history. The signal (kV or pi*k*r^2*h instead of k^2 V) would not misdiagnose a student. No options or predicates are attached.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies the area or volume by k itself
misconceptions.description: The student treats the scale factor as acting directly on the area, surface area or volume, so doubling every length is taken to double the area (or a quarter of every length to make a quarter of the area).
misconceptions.signal: The answer is the scale factor itself: 2 for the surface area of a cone whose radius and height are doubled, 4 for the volume of a prism whose sides are quadrupled, $\frac{1}{3}$ for a circle whose radius becomes a third, $\frac{1}{4}$ for a square whose sides become a quarter.

refutation.text_md: You are thinking that if every length is multiplied by $k$, the area (or volume) is multiplied by $k$ as well. That is true for a length, and finding $k$ from the wording is the first real step, so that part is fine. The slip is that area and volume are not lengths.

An area is built from two lengths multiplied together, so the factor gets applied twice. Take a circle whose radius becomes a third of its size: $A_{\text{new}}=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{9}\pi r^{2}=\frac{1}{9}A$. The new area is $\frac{1}{9}$ of the original, not $\frac{1}{3}$.

The same thing happens with a square whose sides are each a quarter of the original: $A_{\text{new}}=\left(\frac{1}{4}s\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{16}s^{2}=\frac{1}{16}A$. Check it with numbers: a square of side 4 has area 16, and a square of side 1 has area 1, which is $\frac{1}{16}$ of 16, not $\frac{1}{4}$.
A volume is built from three lengths, so the factor is applied three times. When the sides of a triangular prism are quadrupled, $k=4$ and the volume is multiplied by $4^{3}=64$, not by 4.
So after you have found $k$ from the words ("doubled" gives $k=2$, "quadrupled" gives $k=4$), do not stop there. For an area or surface area, work out $k^{2}$. For a volume, work out $k^{3}$.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real and is the direct contrast to the book's k^2 and k^3 rules. I checked each worked figure against the canonical answers: circle with radius a third gives 1/9, square with side a quarter gives 1/16, prism with sides quadrupled gives 64, cone with radius and height doubled gives 4. The signal values (2, 4, 1/3, 1/4) are exactly the unsquared or uncubed k for those questions. The refutation argues against the slip, not just the method. Its numbers are correct and use the book's own calculation, and the side-4 and side-1 square check adds nothing the book does not teach. Step 1 is slightly loose where it says "true for a length", but the next sentence clears it up. No question ids, page numbers, figure numbers or review history appear in the label, description, signal or steps.

covers.text: The scale factor was applied once (k), not squared (k²) — a linear length scaling used for an area

misconceptions.label: Uses k = 3 when a length becomes a third
misconceptions.description: The student reads "a third of its original size" (or a quarter, or half) as a factor of 3 (or 4, or 2) instead of $\frac{1}{3}$, so a shape that gets smaller is given a larger area or volume.
misconceptions.signal: A whole number greater than 1, such as 9 or 16, as the answer to a question in which every length gets smaller, for example 9 for a circle whose radius becomes a third.

refutation.text_md: Your method is right: square $k$ for an area and cube it for a volume. What has flipped is $k$ itself: "a third of its original size" has been read as 3 instead of $\frac{1}{3}$.

$k$ is the number you multiply each original length by to get the new length. A radius that becomes a third of its size is $\frac{1}{3}r$, so $k=\frac{1}{3}$. With $k=3$ the radius would be three times as long as it was.

A quick check is whether the shape gets bigger or smaller. If every length shrinks, the area and the volume must shrink too. Squaring $k=3$ gives 9, which says the circle's area grew ninefold, and that cannot be right for a smaller circle. With $k=\frac{1}{3}$: $A_{\text{new}}=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}r\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{9}\pi r^{2}$, one ninth of the original.

The same applies to the other cases: sides that are a quarter of the size give $k=\frac{1}{4}$ and a new area of $\frac{1}{16}$ of the original, and a radius and height that are both halved give $k=\frac{1}{2}$ and a volume of $\frac{1}{8}$ of the original.

Start by writing down what each length is multiplied by ("doubled" is 2, "a quarter of its size" is $\frac{1}{4}$). Check whether the shape grows or shrinks, then use $k^{2}$ for an area or $k^{3}$ for a volume. The answer should be bigger than 1 only if the shape got bigger.

provenance.verifier_reason: The error is real: reading a third, a quarter or a half as 3, 4 or 2. It is supported by the canonical items for a circle radius a third (1/9), a square side a quarter (1/16) and a cylinder radius and height halved (1/8). The refutation grants the correct method (k^2 or k^3) and attacks only the misreading of k. Every number checks: (1/3)^2=1/9, (1/4)^2=1/16, (1/2)^3=1/8. The grows-or-shrinks sanity check is consistent with the book's answers and adds no new method. It avoids the book's cone-formula slip in the cylinder item and still states the correct 1/8. No ids, pages, figure numbers or review history appear. The signal (a whole number above 1 when everything shrinks, such as 9 or 16) would not misdiagnose a student.

misconceptions.label: Uses the wrong power of k for what is being asked
misconceptions.description: The student chooses $k^{2}$ or $k^{3}$ by the kind of shape instead of by the quantity asked for, typically cubing $k$ for the surface area of a solid or squaring $k$ for a volume.
misconceptions.signal: A surface area answer of $k^{3}$ (8 for a cone whose radius and height are doubled), or a volume answer of $k^{2}$ (16 for a triangular prism whose sides are quadrupled).

refutation.text_md: You know the factor has to be raised to a power, and you have found $k$. The slip is in which power: it depends on what you are asked for (area or volume), not on whether the shape is flat or solid. A cone is a solid, but its surface area is still an area.

The book's rule: when every dimension is multiplied by $k$, an area (including a surface area) is multiplied by $k^{2}$, and a volume is multiplied by $k^{3}$. Surface area is measured in square units and volume in cubic units.

The book puts both on one solid. A prism has volume $493\ \text{cm}^{3}$ and surface area $6007\ \text{cm}^{2}$, and every dimension is multiplied by 4. The volume becomes $493\times4^{3}=31\,552\ \text{cm}^{3}$ and the surface area becomes $6007\times4^{2}=96\,112\ \text{cm}^{2}$. It is the same solid and the same $k$, with two different powers.

Now compare the two answers for a doubled cone and a quadrupled prism. Doubling the cone's radius and height multiplies its surface area by $2^{2}=4$, not by $2^{3}=8$. Quadrupling the sides of a triangular prism multiplies its volume by $4^{3}=64$, not by $4^{2}=16$.
Before you square or cube $k$, ask "is this asking for an area or a volume?" Use $k^{2}$ for surface area and area, and $k^{3}$ for volume.

misconceptions.label: Divides by the outcomes outside the event instead of by all the outcomes
misconceptions.description: The student writes n(E) over the number of outcomes that are not in the event, comparing the event with the rest, instead of over n(S), the total number of outcomes in the sample space.

refutation.text_md: You put the outcomes in the event over the outcomes outside it, which compares one group with the other. Your top number, the count of outcomes in the event, is right. The bottom number is the part to change.

Using the other 8 balls underneath gives $\frac{4}{8}=\frac{1}{2}$, which leaves the blue and white balls out of the total, even though they could be the ball that is picked.

To find $n(S)$, add up every group of outcomes. In a table of colours, that means adding all the counts, not just the ones outside your event. Then count the outcomes in the event for $n(E)$ and write $P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$. Both numbers must come from the same collection of outcomes, with $n(E)$ a part of $n(S)$.

misconceptions.label: Treats outcomes that are not equally likely as if they were
misconceptions.description: The student counts the kinds of result (for example the colours in a bag) as the outcomes and divides by that count, or applies n(E)/n(S) to a situation whose outcomes are not equally likely.

Listing the possible results is the right first move, and the formula $P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ is the right formula. The catch is what you are allowed to count.
$P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ only works when every outcome counted in $n(S)$ is equally likely.

Test it on a bag with $6$ red balls, $3$ blue balls, $2$ green balls and $1$ white ball. Is picking red as likely as picking white? There are six red balls and only one white one, so no. The four colours are not equally likely outcomes, so $\frac{1}{4}$ cannot be the probability of red.

What is equally likely is each individual ball: any one ball is as likely to be picked as any other. So $n(S)=12$ balls and $n(E)=6$ red balls, which gives $P(\text{red})=\frac{6}{12}=\frac{1}{2}$. That is different from $\frac{1}{4}$, and it matches the fact that half the balls are red.

The same warning applies beyond bags. The possible final scores of a soccer match are not all equally likely, so $\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$ cannot be used to find the probability of a team winning. This method does not apply there.

Before you count, ask: is each outcome I am counting as likely as every other one? If yes, use $\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}$. If you listed kinds or categories that are not equally likely, count the outcomes that are, such as each ball rather than each colour, and write $n(E)$ and $n(S)$ from those.

misconceptions.label: Gives a fixed 'expected' value instead of the fraction the trials produced
misconceptions.description: The student treats the relative frequency of an event as one set number, such as 0.5 for heads, and gives that instead of working out the number of trials in which the event occurred divided by the total number of trials, or asks why the answer is not the same every time.

A relative frequency is experimental. It is worked out only from the trials that were actually carried out: the number of trials in which the event occurs, divided by the total number of trials, $f=\frac{p}{t}$.

Compare two coin experiments. A coin tossed $30$ times lands on heads $17$ times, so $f=\frac{17}{30}=0.57$. A coin tossed $44$ times lands on heads $22$ times, so $f=\frac{22}{44}=0.50$. It is the same event with two different relative frequencies, and both are right because each one comes from its own trials.

That is why the book warns that a different relative frequency is possible every time the experiment is repeated: the value depends on the outcomes observed in that run. If you always answered $0.5$, the first coin would be marked wrong, because its trials gave $0.57$.
So read the question for two numbers only: how many trials had the event ($p$) and how many trials there were in all ($t$). Then calculate $\frac{p}{t}$ and round as the question asks.

misconceptions.label: Expects every extra trial to bring the relative frequency closer to the theoretical probability
misconceptions.description: The student reads 'gets closer as the number of trials increases' as 'closer after each single trial', so they expect every new relative frequency to be nearer the theoretical probability than the one before it.

refutation.text_md: You have the main idea right: as the number of trials grows, the relative frequency does end up closer to the theoretical probability. The slip is reading that as 'closer after every single trial'.

The book words it carefully: the relative frequency *tends* to get closer, and it fluctuates, a lot at first and less later. Take the coin tossed $30$ times, where the theoretical probability of heads is $0.5$. After $10$ tosses there were $5$ heads, so $f=\frac{5}{10}=0.50$, exactly the theoretical probability.
The $11$th toss was heads, so $p=6$ and $f=\frac{6}{11}\approx 0.55$. That is further from $0.5$ than before, even though there was one more trial.

It happens at the end too. After $29$ tosses $f=\frac{13}{29}\approx 0.45$. The $30$th toss was tails, so $f=\frac{13}{30}\approx 0.43$, which is further from $0.5$ than the value before it. A single step can go either way, so a value that moves away from the theoretical probability is not a sign you have miscalculated.

When you compare, work out $f=\frac{p}{t}$ after each trial and look at the whole run of values. Say what the run shows: early on $f$ jumps about a lot around the theoretical probability, and as the number of trials increases it fluctuates less and gets closer to it. Do not claim that every new trial is nearer than the last.

misconceptions.label: Reading a group's whole count as its 'only' part
misconceptions.description: The student takes a number given for a whole group, or for the learners taking two subjects together, as if it counted only the people in that group and nowhere else, so the people who also belong to another group get counted twice.

refutation.text_md: You took a number the question gives for a group as if it counted only the part of that group with nothing else in it. Putting each given number straight onto the diagram is a good start. The catch is that a group's number counts everyone in that group, including the people who also belong to another group.

Two groups first. Of $36$ people, $17$ read magazines, $12$ read books and $6$ read both. Those $6$ are inside the $17$ and inside the $12$, so only $17-6=11$ read only magazines and only $12-6=6$ read only books.
So $36-17-12=7$ takes the $6$ who read both away twice. Adding the regions instead: $11+6+6=23$ read magazines or books or both, and $36-23=13$ read neither.

Three groups work the same way. "$16$ take Maths and History" includes some learners who take Geography too. Let $x$ be the number who take all three subjects. Then $16-x$ take Maths and History but not Geography, and $6-x$ take Geography and History but not Maths.

Writing $16$ and $6$ whole into those two parts cannot be right. The History circle would hold $16+16+6=38$ learners before anyone who takes all three is counted, yet only $36$ take History. Adding the History regions with $x$ kept in gives $36=16+(16-x)+(6-x)+x$, so $x=2$: $14$ take Maths and History but not Geography, and $4$ take Geography and History but not Maths.

Next time a question gives a number for a group, or for two groups together, write it as the sum of the regions inside it. Then check that the regions in each circle add back up to the number you were given.

misconceptions.label: Gives one whole event set instead of the shared elements
misconceptions.description: The student writes out every element of one event set ($A$ or $B$) and calls that the intersection, instead of keeping only the elements that are also in the other set.

refutation.text_md: You found the right numbers to start from: the shared elements are in your list, and you looked in the right place. The slip is writing out a whole event set ($B$, or $A$) and calling it $A\cap B$. A whole set holds every one of its elements, shared or not.
$A\cap B$ means only the elements that are in both $A$ and $B$. So a number has to pass two checks: it is in $A$, and it is in $B$. One check is not enough.

Try it on an example where $B$ is $\{7, 10, 11\}$ and $A$ also contains 7 and 10, along with other numbers. Check each number of $B$ against $A$. 7 is in $A$, so it stays. 10 is in $A$, so it stays. 11 is not in $A$, so it fails and is left out.

That leaves $A\cap B=\{7, 10\}$. The list $\{7, 10, 11\}$ is just $B$ with nothing removed, so it is not the intersection. The same goes for writing out all of $A$: numbers that sit only in $A$ fail the check for $B$.
Next time, take one event set and go through its elements one by one, asking "is it in the other set too?" Write down only the ones that get a yes. That list is $A\cap B$.

misconceptions.label: Adds the two probabilities and forgets what is in both events
misconceptions.description: The student finds P(A) and P(B) and adds them, without subtracting P(A∩B), so every outcome that lies in both events is counted twice.
misconceptions.signal: The answer is exactly P(A) + P(B) even though the two events share at least one outcome, for example 17/52 for 'a diamond or a three'.

refutation.text_md: You added $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ and stopped there. Adding is the right way to start, because the union is made of everything in $A$ and everything in $B$. The catch is that an outcome sitting in both events has been counted twice.

Try it on a card drawn from an ordinary pack of $52$ cards, asking for a diamond or a three. There are $13$ diamonds and $4$ threes, so adding the probabilities gives $\frac{13}{52}+\frac{4}{52}=\frac{17}{52}$.

But the three of diamonds is one of the $13$ diamonds and also one of the $4$ threes, so the sum counted that card twice. Only $16$ different cards are a diamond or a three, and the answer is $\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}$, not $\frac{17}{52}$.

That is the reason the identity has a third term: $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. The only card in both events is the three of diamonds, so $n(A\cap B)=1$ and $P(A\cap B)=\frac{1}{52}$. Then $\frac{13}{52}+\frac{4}{52}-\frac{1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}$.

Each time you work out $P(A)$ and $P(B)$, also look for what is in both events and work out $P(A\cap B)=\frac{n(A\cap B)}{n(S)}$, then subtract it. When $A\cap B$ is empty, as with the event sets $\{1,2,5,6\}$ and $\{3\}$ on a six-number sample space, $P(A\cap B)=0$ and the subtraction changes nothing. That is why adding alone gave the right answer there.

The refutation uses the book's identity and its P(A∩B) = n(A∩B)/n(S) form. It argues against the error by showing the double count and why the third term exists, and does not just restate the method. It names no question id, page, figure or review history. The last step spells out the event sets of the other example, so a student can follow it without having seen that question.
